segments.ko: 진, 그런 메시지를 들을 때 왜 거부감이 드는지 물어봐도 될까요? 그들은 우리 생명을 구하려고 하는 건데, 어떻게 거기에 거부감을 느낄 수 있죠?
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: When I started running, I didn't start being able to run until I was in a neighborhood where there were spaces to run.
segments.ko: 제가 달리기를 시작했을 때, 달릴 수 있는 공간이 있는 동네에 살기 전까지는 제대로 시작도 못 했거든요.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: I remember like, I grew up in South Philly. I tried to run in my neighborhood, Washington Avenue, but it was all just like factories and the streets messed up.
segments.ko: 사우스 필라델피아에서 자랐을 때가 기억나네요. 우리 동네 워싱턴 애비뉴에서 달리려고 해봤지만, 온통 공장뿐이고 길도 엉망이었죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: Like I didn't have running shoes. You know what I mean? Like all those things, the barriers to entry, right?
segments.ko: 러닝화도 없었고요. 제 말 무슨 뜻인지 아시죠? 진입 장벽 같은 거요, 그렇죠?
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: And I didn't know what I was doing. I was a teenager, but when I started running and earnest in my 20s, I was in a neighborhood that I was close to Prospect Park.
segments.ko: 어떻게 해야 할지도 몰랐어요. 십 대였으니까요. 하지만 20대에 본격적으로 달리기를 시작했을 때는 프로스펙트 공원 근처 동네에 살고 있었죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: I had a running store in between my house and the park. If I needed new sneakers, I could get fitted for new sneakers. It was a whole process.
segments.ko: 집과 공원 사이에 러닝 전문점도 있었고요. 새 운동화가 필요하면 발에 맞춰서 살 수도 있었죠. 그건 하나의 과정이었어요.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: There's all these barriers to entry, two things. Like, oh, you want to be fit? Go run. You want to be strong. Go to the gym.
segments.ko: 이런 모든 진입 장벽이 있는데, 사람들은 '건강해지고 싶어? 그럼 달려. 강해지고 싶어? 그럼 체육관에 가'라고 간단히 말하죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: Running is maybe one of the most democratic, small D democratic ways you can be active. And there's a barrier to entry.
segments.ko: 달리기는 아마도 가장 민주적인 활동 방식 중 하나일 겁니다. 하지만 거기에도 진입 장벽이 존재하죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: running, you have to live in a place where there's like the physical infrastructure to do it, where the streets are safe.
segments.ko: 달리기를 하려면 그걸 할 수 있는 물리적 인프라가 있고 거리가 안전한 곳에 살아야 하니까요.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: Yeah, it's different. Yeah, I would also add that being able to run or being able to walk is very much based on ability. Ability, absolutely.
segments.ko: 네, 맞아요. 달릴 수 있거나 걸을 수 있다는 것 자체가 신체적 능력에 크게 좌우된다는 점도 덧붙이고 싶네요. 능력 말이죠, 전적으로 동감합니다.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: Right? And it makes sense that it would sort of activate some discomfort.
segments.ko: 그렇죠? 그래서 어느 정도 불편함을 느끼는 게 당연합니다.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: And I think in the context of we saw Black people in class in general, it was like, I do think there's a lot of times when and middle class black people are sort of making pronouncements about what black folks
segments.ko: 그리고 전반적으로 흑인 계층의 맥락에서 보면, 중산층 흑인들이 흑인 대중에게 훈수를 두는 경우가 많다고 생각합니다.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: and the aspirational black folks in particular are saying, like, this is what we need as a people. It's always like, just be more like us.
segments.ko: 특히 성공을 꿈꾸는 흑인들이 '이게 우리 민족에게 필요한 거야'라고 말하는 건, 항상 '그냥 우리처럼 해봐'라는 식이죠.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: Just be more, comport yourself in a more middle class way. And it's like, I don't have those things. I can't just like pretend to be a Huxtable.
segments.ko: 그냥 좀 더 중산층답게 처신하라는 건데, 사실 난 그런 게 없거든요. 그냥 헉스터블 가족(부유한 흑인 가정)인 척할 수는 없잖아요.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: I don't have any of the things that are looking to be a Huxtable exactly. Yes, the accoutrements. Yeah, I agree.
segments.ko: 헉스터블처럼 보일 수 있는 조건이 아무것도 없단 말이죠. 네, 그런 부수적인 조건들이요. 맞아요, 동감합니다.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: So class is really complicated when you're talking about black people because class is not just about your relationship to the means of production for black people.
segments.ko: 흑인에 대해 이야기할 때 계급은 정말 복잡합니다. 흑인들에게 계급은 단순히 생산 수단과의 관계만을 의미하지 않기 때문이죠.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: Class is also about aspiration. So it's about how you carry yourself, what your values are, how you raise your children. Do you hang out on your stoop? Do you go to the juke joint?
segments.ko: 계급은 열망에 관한 것이기도 합니다. 어떻게 처신하는지, 가치관은 무엇인지, 아이를 어떻게 키우는지 같은 거죠. 현관 계단에 앉아 시간을 보내는지, 아니면 술집에 가는지 같은 거요.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: That's also about class as well. Right? So, you know, you had sort of aspiring class, middle class, black people who very much espoused this idea that we need to exercise.
segments.ko: 그것도 계급에 관한 것입니다. 그렇죠? 그래서 운동을 해야 한다는 생각을 강력하게 옹호했던 중산층 혹은 그를 꿈꾸는 흑인들이 있었던 거죠.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: We need to aspire toward fitness because it's good for racial uplift. It's actually good in terms of its health benefits. It will allow us to survive all of this violence that we are experiencing.
segments.ko: 인종적 지위 향상에 도움이 되니까 피트니스를 지향해야 한다는 거죠. 건강에도 실제로 좋고요. 우리가 겪고 있는 이 모든 폭력 속에서 살아남게 해줄 테니까요.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: And it will allow us to demonstrate our fitness for citizenship. So if we are in shape, if we are like, and as you said, also a solid moral character,
segments.ko: 그리고 그것은 우리가 시민으로서 적합하다는 것을 증명하게 해줄 겁니다. 우리가 좋은 체격을 갖고, 말씀하신 대로 확고한 도덕적 인품을 갖춘다면 말이죠.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: we will prove ourselves to be like upright citizens and worthy of the wall of protections that come with being an American citizen.
segments.ko: 우리가 올바른 시민임을 증명하고 미국 시민으로서 누릴 수 있는 보호 장벽을 가질 자격이 있음을 보여줄 수 있다는 거죠.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: Going back to what you said about like the way that we think about fitness, the way it's conceived as like something you did outside of work in your leisure time, right?
segments.ko: 우리가 피트니스를 생각하는 방식, 즉 일터 밖의 여가 시간에 하는 무언가로 인식하는 방식에 대해 하신 말씀으로 돌아가 볼까요?
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: Like you think about, I don't know, like the Central American day laborers at the Home Depot, who were like to do their jobs, you have to be incredibly strong, right? You have to be in a crazy shape to do it.
segments.ko: 홈디포 앞에 있는 중미 출신 일용직 노동자들을 생각해 보세요. 그 일을 하려면 엄청나게 힘이 세야 하잖아요? 정말 대단한 체력이 필요하죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: Yes. But I don't think people think of them as like sort of like paragons or even just like examples of really fit people.
segments.ko: 맞아요. 하지만 사람들이 그들을 피트니스의 귀감이나 체력이 정말 좋은 사람의 예시로 생각하지는 않는 것 같아요.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: Gene, exactly. And I would be remiss to not say that in the era of slavery, one of the biggest sort of lies about African Americans, black people who were enslaved is that they were lazy.
segments.ko: 진, 바로 그겁니다. 노예제 시대에 노예가 된 흑인들에 대한 가장 큰 거짓말 중 하나가 그들이 게으르다는 것이었다는 점을 꼭 말하고 싶네요.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: I want you to imagine a planter, a slaveholder, is writing in his diary. These people are lazy and they are working from sun up to sundown. They're lazy.
segments.ko: 한 농장주가 일기에 이렇게 쓴다고 상상해 보세요. '이 사람들은 게으르다.' 그런데 그들은 해 뜰 때부터 해 질 때까지 일하고 있어요. 그래도 게으르다는 거죠.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: And that is a trope we still live with today that began at that time as they were tirelessly seriously laboring.
segments.ko: 그들이 지치지 않고 심각하게 노동하던 그 시절에 시작된 그 고정관념이 오늘날까지도 우리 곁에 남아 있는 겁니다.
segments.speaker: Eva Perkins

segments.en: Alright y'all, cards on the table. I am a gym rat. It's been such an ingrained part of my life for so long that I don't even really think about it anymore, right?
segments.ko: 여러분, 솔직히 고백하자면 저는 운동광입니다. 아주 오랫동안 제 삶의 깊숙한 부분이어서 이제는 별로 생각조차 안 할 정도예요.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: But when we were talking, Eva Perkins asked me a real straightforward question, how would I define fitness? And like, I haven't anything close to a coherent answer, which is wild, right?
segments.ko: 그런데 우리가 대화할 때 에바 퍼킨스가 제게 아주 단도직입적인 질문을 던졌어요. 피트니스를 어떻게 정의하겠느냐고요. 그런데 일관성 있는 답변 근처에도 못 갔죠. 정말 황당하죠?
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: Like I spent decades of my life, God knows how much money at this point running and lifting and overcoming and working my way back from injuries, trying to be fit
segments.ko: 인생의 수십 년을 바쳤고, 달리고 무게를 들고 부상을 극복하며 몸을 만들기 위해 쓴 돈이 얼마인지도 모를 정도인데 말이죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: or to get to some ideal fit version of myself, which I don't think I will ever get to. I don't even think I've thought through what would be on the other side of that thing if I got there, you know, it's just this moving target in my head.
segments.ko: 절대 도달할 수 없을 것 같은 이상적인 내 모습이 되려고 노력해 왔어요. 만약 도달한다 해도 그 너머에 무엇이 있을지조차 생각해 본 적이 없어요. 그냥 제 머릿속에서 계속 변하는 목표일 뿐이죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: And I think a lot of people who are gym rats feel this way. Like, look at Hasan, right? Like, he is tall, he is confident, he's yoked,
segments.ko: 많은 운동광들이 이렇게 느낄 것 같아요. 하산을 보세요. 키도 크고 자신감 넘치고 근육질이죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: he is somebody to me who is pretty objectively a fit person, but he feels like he is not where he wants to be.
segments.ko: 제 눈에는 객관적으로 아주 건강하고 좋은 몸을 가진 사람이지만, 그는 여전히 자신이 원하는 수준에 도달하지 못했다고 느껴요.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: My physical fitness is always top of mind. I always have that hunger in the back of my mind. I always want to improve myself.
segments.ko: 제 신체적 건강은 항상 최우선 순위입니다. 마음 한구석에는 항상 갈망이 있어요. 항상 더 나아지고 싶죠.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: It's constantly eating away in my mind that I'm not doing enough. Like I'll tell you right now. Every time I play basketball, I'm checking my heart rate religiously.
segments.ko: 충분히 하지 않고 있다는 생각이 계속 절 괴롭혀요. 지금도 말씀드릴 수 있는데, 농구를 할 때마다 강박적으로 심박수를 체크합니다.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: And as of late, I think it's like zone four. If I'm not mistaken, like that's, yeah. So that's unacceptable. Like, and I'm, you know, right now, even when we're having this conversation
segments.ko: 최근에는 심박수가 존 4까지 올라가는 것 같아요. 제 기억이 맞는다면요. 그건 용납할 수 없는 수준이에요. 지금 우리가 대화를 나누는 중에도...
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: or even when I'm in the shower, and perhaps for the rest of the day, that's going to be eating away at the back of my mind. Like, how do I fix that. How do I get my cardio up?
segments.ko: 혹은 샤워를 할 때나 아마 오늘 남은 시간 내내 머릿속을 맴돌 겁니다. 어떻게 하면 그걸 고칠 수 있을까? 어떻게 심폐 지구력을 올릴 수 있을까 하고요.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: I was a deeply insecure person. I had, you know, I still have body dysmorphia. I'm pretty open about my insecurities as well.
segments.ko: 저는 깊은 자격지심이 있는 사람이었어요. 신체 변형 장애도 있었고 지금도 그렇고요. 제 결핍에 대해서도 상당히 개방적입니다.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: Obviously, it's much easier for me to be confident certainly at this point in my life, especially. I mean, I'm successful. I'm six four
segments.ko: 물론 지금 제 인생의 이 시점에서 자신감을 갖는 게 훨씬 쉽긴 하죠. 성공도 했고 키도 193cm니까요.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: having said that confidence is something that you develop internally. And my journey to developing confidence actually came from my fitness journey.
segments.ko: 그렇긴 해도 자신감이란 내면에서 길러지는 것입니다. 사실 제가 자신감을 갖게 된 여정은 제 피트니스 여정에서 시작되었어요.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: There was this goal I wanted to attain my entire life. I always wanted to be healthy. I wanted to have a six pack.
segments.ko: 평생 달성하고 싶었던 목표가 있었어요. 항상 건강하고 싶었고 식스팩을 갖고 싶었죠.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: It'll come across as funny this admission for many people because everybody like what? That's your goal. That's what you will like wanted to accomplish. Like that's such a silly goal.
segments.ko: 이런 고백이 많은 사람에게는 웃기게 들릴 수도 있어요. 다들 '뭐? 그게 네 목표라고? 네가 이루고 싶었던 게 그거야? 정말 바보 같은 목표네'라고 하겠죠.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: But for me, young boy growing up in Turkey, very fat, my whole family is obese. I just, I tried so hard and it was such a massive weight on my shoulders all the time.
segments.ko: 하지만 터키에서 자라며 아주 뚱뚱했고 온 가족이 비만이었던 어린 저에게는 정말 간절한 목표였고 항상 어깨를 짓누르는 큰 짐이었어요.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: So the way that I was able to achieve that was through consistency to have this like work ethic, this, this rigid work structure that I existed in and still exist in.
segments.ko: 그래서 제가 그걸 이룰 수 있었던 방법은 꾸준함, 즉 제가 지켜왔고 지금도 지키고 있는 엄격한 노동 윤리와 구조를 유지하는 것이었습니다.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: I now know that as long as I work hard, I can achieve anything.
segments.ko: 이제 저는 열심히 노력하기만 하면 무엇이든 이룰 수 있다는 걸 압니다.
segments.speaker: Hasan Piker

segments.en: So I talked to Hasan because he works out obviously, but Natalia is a Hyrox coach. She was actually doing her ninth Hyrox the day after we talked.
segments.ko: 하산은 당연히 운동을 하니까 이야기를 나눴지만, 나탈리아는 하이록스 코치이기도 합니다. 우리가 대화한 다음 날 그녀의 아홉 번째 하이록스 경기가 있었죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: Eva is a back squat girl. She loves strength training. These people are not just studying this, that this is a big part of their lives. They live it.
segments.ko: 에바는 백 스쿼트를 즐깁니다. 근력 운동을 아주 좋아하죠. 이 사람들은 단순히 이걸 연구만 하는 게 아니라, 그들의 삶의 큰 부분을 차지하고 있습니다. 몸소 실천하고 있죠.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: And all of us, including me too, are kind of working through this relationship we have with our bodies and in the gym, I guess, in the work we place on the effort we put into our bodies.
segments.ko: 저를 포함한 우리 모두는 자신의 몸, 그리고 체육관과의 관계, 그리고 우리 몸에 들이는 노력에 대해 계속 고민하고 있습니다.
segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: I think one of the reasons that fitness endures is such a central part of American life and things that make people think you're a good person if you run marathons or you go to the gym every day,
segments.ko: 피트니스가 미국인의 삶에서 중심적인 부분으로 남은 이유 중 하나는, 매일 마라톤을 하거나 체육관에 가면 그 사람을 좋은 사람이라고 생각하게 만들기 때문인 것 같아요.
segments.speaker: Natalia Mehlman Petrzela

segments.en: And so I think that we gravitate towards these stories of like meritocracy and, you know, good things, whether it's a fit body or some accolade.

segments.en: And fitness really shows that Americans love hard work. We love stories about being self-made.

segments.en: When I first asked Natalia about fitness and fascism, she said there were two ways to think about it.

segments.speaker: Natalia Mehlman Petrzela

segments.en: Okay, so there's the big systemic ways that our bodies are useful to the state. But then there's the more personal intimate ways that these ideas can creep in, what she calls body fascism.

segments.speaker: Natalia Mehlman Petrzela

segments.en: Which is the idea that like, like the fitness industry and fitness culture actually serves to kind of impose these impossible body standards on people that elevates and kind of like lionizes people who have very particular bodies

segments.en: and determines that the other people are kind of useless. We display and we cultivate and we value our fittest citizens and then what happens by implication or explicitly?

segments.speaker: Natalia Mehlman Petrzela

segments.en: Well, it's this very eugenic project, right? That the people who are weak or disabled or can't cut it, they are seen as expendable.

segments.en: Wanting to be fit and not even really being able to identify what that might even mean leaves this huge open space that makes us really suggestible and vulnerable to all kinds of ideas and ideologies.

segments.en: Like when a trainer or spin instructor is yelling at you, what is your why? They are shouting into that space.

segments.en: And if I'm really honest, like, I worry that if I peel back, like all the layers of why I work out, like what I find there might be kind of ugly.

segments.speaker: Gene Demby

segments.en: I would argue that fitness cannot be embodied because it is so theoretical and immaterial and elusive.
